new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand phonological statement found describes Kihung'an as a tone language with three marked levels (high, low, mid); no source opened says anything about word stress. The article's 'stress-focus' is a term for English; the Kihung'an equivalent is 'tone-focus', i.e. focus marked by tonal change, not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; footnote 4 (p. 262) notes that the final vowel is almost always deleted except in certain environments, which bears on word shape but not on stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tones are marked on words inside sentence examples in a syntax article; there is no phonology section and no discussion of citation forms or phrase-level prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Takizala's 'Kihung'an' [kíhùŋàn], Torday & Joyce's 'Ba-Huana', and Bostoen & Koni Muluwa's 'Hungan (H42)' all map to hung1278 (ISO hum). Bostoen & Koni Muluwa 2011 single out the Kipuka variety (new 7-vowel system); Mwemfu 1996 contrasts the Kwenge and Vanga parlers; Bastin et al. 1999 sample three Hungana points (Lundu, Bulungu, unspecified). No separate glottocodes exist for these varieties.

sources.locator: p. 259, footnote 1 (PDF p. 1 of the extracted article; p. 99 of)
sources.note: Syntax article. The only phonological statement is footnote 1 (p. 259): Kihung'an is a Bantu language and the author marks HIGH, LOW and MID tone. No statement on word stress anywhere; 'stress-focus' in the paper refers to English, and the Kihung'an counterpart is called 'tone-focus'. Footnote 4 (p. 262) adds that the final vowel is almost always deleted.
